chunk_findings.detail: The new bucketing treats only `state == "running"` as "keep in full", so every job whose status is `"elsewhere"` (unended job started on another host — the state that carries the tail text "check it on that host") is pushed into `others` and therefore collapsed or dropped. That contradicts both the change's own docstring ("exited or killed jobs of OTHER items" collapse) and the README addition ("Running jobs … are listed in full"): an `elsewhere` job is *not* exited or killed, it is alive/unverifiable on another host, which is exactly the case the existing tail text exists to warn about ("WAIT for it; do not start it again" / "check it on that host"). Concrete input: `state.jobs` holds 7 unended jobs — one belonging to `B-mine`, six belonging to other items that were launched on host H2, so `J.status(j).state == "elsewhere"` for those six (this brief runs on H1). Running `ddflow brief --item B-mine` gives `keep = 0`, so all six go into `others`, `hidden = 6`, and the output is the item's own job plus the line "- _6 more unended job(s) (other items', not running): `ddflow job list` shows them…_". The alive-on-H2 jobs — and the "check it on that host"/do-not-restart warning the original code printed for each — vanish entirely, even though under the stated rule ("the item's own jobs and **running** ones in full") they should have been listed. The same misclassification bites a plain `brief`: with more than `BRIEF_OTHER_JOBS` `elsewhere` jobs, the oldest of these alive-but-unverified jobs are silently folded into the "(older, not running)" count line.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py::_brief_jobs (the `s.state == "running"` classification)

chunk_findings.detail: The new partition treats only the literal state `"running"` as "must be shown in full"; every other unended state is dropped into `others`. But the status map used two lines below acknowledges a fourth state, `"elsewhere"` (tail text "check it on that host"), which is precisely a job that was started on another host and whose liveness cannot be verified from here — i.e. an unended job that may still be running. Concrete case: a job `B-other` registered on host `buildbox` is still running remotely (state `"elsewhere"`), and the user runs `ddflow brief --item B-af-signals`. With `item` set, `keep == 0`, so `B-other` is classified as an "other" and never enters `shown`; the brief emits only the count line `_N more unended job(s) (other items', not running): ddflow job list shows them...`. The job's `ELSEWHERE ... check it on that host` line and its warning are gone, and the count line asserts it is "not running" when in fact liveness is unknown/possibly live — exactly the case the docstring says is "the most expensive thing to restart by accident". Before the change every unended job was printed, so this is a new information loss for remote jobs, not just a collapse of exited/gone ones.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py — `_brief_jobs` classification `s.state == "running"`

chunk_findings.detail: `_project` creates all 40 “other” jobs with `"pid": 0` and states in the comment that this means “never running”. That premise is unsafe: `pid 0` is not a sentinel for a dead process. A standard liveness check such as `os.kill(pid, 0)` succeeds for pid 0, because the call targets the caller’s process group. If the implementation detects running jobs that way, every ONE of the OTHER jobs will be classified as running; the fix’s intended behaviour is to list running jobs in full, so `Jother000` will appear in the brief and the assertion `assert "Jother000" not in text` (and the `f"{STALE} more unended job(s)"` collapse assertion) will fail on correct code. The test should use a pid that reliably raises `ProcessLookupError` (e.g., a large unused pid) or mock the liveness check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_brief_jobs_budget.py:_project

chunk_findings.detail: The change moves every job whose status is `"elsewhere"` into the "shown in full" set unconditionally: `live = s.state in ("running", "elsewhere")` and then `shown if live or (item and j.item == item) else others`. Because `live` is ORed in, it bypasses the per-item filter entirely — a job that is on another host *and belongs to some other item* is still emitted in full, even when the brief is about a specific item. That contradicts the expected behaviour stated for this fix ("jobs of the current item (and running ones) in full, the rest collapsed to a count line naming `ddflow job list`") and re-creates the exact failure B8114a8b531 was filed for: with `brief --item B-af-signals` in a project where unrelated items have a backlog of unended jobs registered on another host (e.g. jobs added with `--pid` on a build box), all of those jobs print as `## Long-running jobs` lines ahead of the current item's section, pushing its decisions/rules/lessons past `session.brief_max_tokens` and truncating the brief. Only the `item`-matching jobs and genuinely-running jobs should be exempt from the collapse; "not checkable here" is not the same as "about the asked-for item", so the rest (including other items' elsewhere jobs) should fall into the count line.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:777 (`_brief_jobs`)

chunk_findings.detail: Unended jobs whose `host` differs from the local host are always rendered in full, so the crowding/truncation the fix targets recurs whenever the stale jobs came from another host — the case where the job can never receive a local `job.ended` and thus never stops being "unended". Input: 33 unended jobs of other items with `host="other"` → 33 `- **` lines before `_brief_current` → the brief is still cut at 1200 tokens before the current item's sections, and the "more unended job(s) / `ddflow job list`" collapse line does not bound them (the test shows an unrelated item's job printed in full while only the local-host ones are counted). If the fix is meant to guarantee "the rest collapsed to a count line", the collapse decision must be based on the current item plus a positive running signal, not on a host-value exemption.

chunk_findings.detail: The change promotes every unended job whose status is `elsewhere` into the fully-listed `shown` set, for every brief and regardless of which item the job belongs to. `elsewhere` is, per the added comment, the state for "not checkable here" — i.e. a job launched from another host (the same diff's README sentence is the only justification for it). Such a job is never re-resolved locally and never leaves the pending set until someone records `ddflow job end`, so on a project whose jobs are started from more than one host, the set of `elsewhere` jobs grows without bound and is *not* counted in the collapsed `hidden` line. Concretely: `ddflow brief --item B-af-signals` against a store containing 30 old `elsewhere` jobs of `fix-Ba0904a2430`, `B-dupes-sweep`, `B-onboard-*`, ... now emits 30 job lines ahead of `_brief_current`, and with `session.brief_max_tokens=1200` the brief is again truncated before the asked-for item's decisions, rules and lessons — precisely bug B8114a8b531. The same change's own README claim that "a backlog of uncollected jobs never pushes the item's own section out of the token budget" is therefore false for this class: the fix reduces crowding for locally-checkable jobs while re-opening it for jobs on another host.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_doc()` entry documents the default for `schedule.parallel` as `"fixed"`:

```python
"schedule.parallel": (
    "fixed",
    "no safety dimension; changes least -- max_parallel_tasks is the number, nothing adapts",
),
```

but the change's stated (and failing-first-tested) default is `parallel = "auto"` ("defaults load as auto/4/2/8", "parallel absent = auto"). Every other entry in this `_doc` table pairs the tuple's first element with the knob's actual default (`schedule.empty_phase` → `problem`, `enforce.commit_without_lease` → `block`, `dedupe.on_match` → `ask`, etc.), and the reason string here ("changes least -- ... nothing adapts") describes `fixed`, not `auto`. So on a config with no `schedule.parallel` key, the effective behavior is `auto` (adaptive), yet `ddflow config --explain` (and any consumer that reads the first element as the documented default) reports `fixed`. Input: a fresh `ddflow init` / old config with no `schedule.parallel`; expected explain output `auto`, actual `fixed`. The entry should read `"auto"`, or the actual default and the test expectation must be changed to `fixed`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config.py `_doc()["schedule.parallel"]`

chunk_findings.detail: `params()` never reads `cfg.schedule.parallel`, so a `fixed` schedule is translated into the same adaptive parameter set as `auto`. Given `[schedule] parallel = "fixed"`, `max_parallel_tasks = 4` and the shipped defaults `max_parallel_min = 2`, `max_parallel_max = 8`, `adapt_up_after_s = 600`, the function returns `FC.Params(start=4, floor=2, ceiling=8, adapt_up_after_s=600, ...)`. Any caller that folds through this function (the module docstring calls it "the one place that turns the operator's knobs into its Params, so every caller ... folds with the same numbers") therefore hands the controller a movable range `[2, 8]` even though the operator selected a fixed limit; after `adapt_up_after_s` the controller may raise the limit to 8 (or lower it to 2), which contradicts the stated requirement that "fixed + 4 reproduces the old behaviour" (no adaptation, hard limit 4). The validation rules quoted in the intent only enforce `auto|fixed` and `min <= start <= max`, so nothing else pins `floor == ceiling` for fixed mode. To honour the knob, `params()` has to special-case `s.parallel != "auto"` (e.g. `floor = ceiling = s.max_parallel_tasks`, and derive `quiet_after_decrease_s`/`cooldown_s` so no movement occurs), or the caller must avoid building adaptive `Params` for a fixed config — neither is present in the reviewed code.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_range_problems` swallows every `Exception` with `return set()`, and its stated justification ("a text that does not load is Config.check's to report") is false at both call sites: the function is only invoked *after* `tomllib.loads` + `Config.check` have already succeeded. So any exception that escapes here is either a real bug or an unexpectedly unloadable *merged* config, not a load error, and it is silently converted into "this text has no range problems". Because callers then do `after - before`, the empty set is asymmetric and produces two concrete wrong outcomes:

1. If the "before" side raises while the "after" side succeeds, `after - set()` is the *entire* problem set of the effective config, so every pre-existing inconsistency is reclassified as "new" and an unrelated edit is refused — the exact opposite of the documented "a project whose range was already inconsistent can still make an unrelated edit, or the repair". If the "after" side raises while "before" succeeds, `new_range = set() - before` is empty and a genuinely newly inconsistent edit (e.g. `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 999`, giving `start > max` in the merged config) is accepted, writing a config that later commands must reject — i.e. the range guard is silently disabled exactly when it is supposed to fire.

`parallel_range_problems` and `_effective` are the only things reachable here; a bug or a cross-layer failure in either should surface, not be reported as "no problems". chunk_findings.detail: The new doctor advisories decide whether a cap is "explicit" with `_explicit`, which is true for *any* non-default source layer (`cfg.sources.get(key, "default") != "default"`), including the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer. But the remedy command they emit is layer-blind: it always writes the committed layer. Concretely, take a 4-core machine whose machine sizing was put in the local layer as instructed (`ddflow config --local --set worktree.max_parallel 4`). `_explicit` returns true and the value equals `OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT`, so the finding fires and prints "`ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` follows the schedule limit instead". Running exactly that command writes `.ddflow/config.toml` to 0, but the local layer wins for sizing, so `cfg.worktree.max_parallel` stays 4: the auto cap is unchanged and the doctor keeps firing forever with a command that cannot silence it. The remedy needs to target the layer the value actually lives in (e.g. `ddflow config --local --set worktree.max_parallel 0` when the source is the local layer). The same applies to the `schedule.max_parallel_tasks` advisory: "to accept auto, remove the line" is a no-op when the explicit 4 is in the local layer, and re-running `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks ...` on the committed file would not override it either.

chunk_findings.detail: Every entry in this `(value, why)` doc table pairs a knob with its shipped default and a sentence describing what that default does: `schedule.cycle_policy` → `("error", …)`, `schedule.unknown_dep_policy` → `("block", …)`, `schedule.empty_phase` → `("problem", …)`, `dedupe.on_match` → `("ask", …)`, `enforce.commit_without_lease` → `("block", …)` — in each case the first element is exactly the default the package ships. The change under review, however, registers `"schedule.parallel": ("fixed", "no safety dimension; changes least -- max_parallel_tasks is the number, nothing adapts")`, while the intent and the choice tuple added two lines earlier (`("auto", "fixed")`) define the default as `auto`. So `ddflow config --explain` will report `schedule.parallel`'s default as `fixed`, i.e. it will tell users that adaptation is off by default when the shipped default is `auto`; and any doc-coverage check that cross-validates the documented value against the `ScheduleConfig` default (or against the first member of the choices tuple) is comparing `fixed` to `auto` and cannot pass. The fix is to make the pair `("auto", …)` with a sentence describing the auto default.

chunk_findings.detail: `params()` never reads `cfg.schedule.parallel`, so it cannot encode the required "fixed" semantics (intent: `parallel` is `auto|fixed`; `max_parallel_tasks` is "the start value in auto, **the number in fixed**", and "fixed + 4 reproduces the old behaviour"). Given a config with `parallel = "fixed"`, `max_parallel_tasks = 4`, `max_parallel_min = 2`, `max_parallel_max = 8`, the call returns `FC.Params(start=4, floor=2, ceiling=8, ...)`, i.e. a controller that is free to move the limit anywhere in `[2, 8]`. The operator asked for exactly 4, so the run does not reproduce the old fixed-4 behaviour and can exceed or fall below it. The module's own docstring says this is "the one place that turns the operator's knobs into its `Params`, so every caller (the sampler, `plan`, the operator surface) folds with the same numbers" — meaning fixed mode must be neutralised here (e.g. `floor=ceiling=start` when `s.parallel == "fixed"`); nothing else in this change does it, and the corresponding `fixed + 4` acceptance test cannot pass through this path.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_explicit()` returns True for a key whose source is anything other than `"default"`, including a value that lives in the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer. The advisory's remedy, however, is always the non-`--local` command:

```
"... clean it ... `ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` follows the schedule limit instead ..."
```

Since the change itself establishes that "a local-layer value overrides the committed one" and that `--local` is what selects the local layer, running `ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` writes the committed layer while the local `worktree.max_parallel = 4` still wins. Concrete scenario: a machine has `[worktree] max_parallel = 4` only in `.ddflow/local` (exactly the "machine-specific value goes to the local layer" case the intent prescribes). On that host the effective `cfg.worktree.max_parallel` is 4 and its source is `local`, so this finding fires and prints the remedy. The operator runs it, no error is reported, and the cap silently stays at 4 — the doctor claims to have given "the exact remedy command" but the command is a no-op for this input. The same defect applies to the `max_parallel_tasks` advisory ("to accept auto, remove the line"): when the old explicit 4 lives in the local layer, removing the committed line does nothing. The code has the source string available (it was just used by `_explicit`) but never uses it to pick `--local` in the message.

chunk_findings.detail: The edited tests inject `max_parallel_tasks = 1` into `[schedule]` while leaving the shipped default `max_parallel_min = 2` in place. The change's own stated validation is "min<=start<=max, min>=1; invalid -> config error exit 3 naming the key", and `max_parallel_tasks` is the start value in `parallel='auto'` (which is exactly what these tests rely on, since they only add the one key). With start=1 and min=2 the config is invalid, so `run_cli(...)` will exit 3 at config load and none of the assertions that follow (claim U1 succeeds, U2/U3 are refused, "any release frees a slot", word-for-word cap wording, etc.) can run; the tests `"N more are ready" read as a contradiction` and the `_blocking_leases` wording test cannot exercise the cap-1 case at all. If instead the implementation silently clamps the start up into `[min,max]`, the effective cap becomes 2, which is equally wrong for these tests' expectation of a single startable item. Either way these hunks are only correct if `max_parallel_min` is also lowered to 1 (e.g. add `max_parallel_min = 1` alongside `max_parallel_tasks = 1`), which the diff does not do.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. Concrete scenario: editing the committed layer with `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` while the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer is unreadable (`chmod 000`) or malformed; the edited text passes `Config.check`, then `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` merges the broken local layer and raises `OSError`/`ValueError`, which now propagates out of `_new_range_problems` uncaught instead of being swallowed. Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The detail string for the explicit-`max_parallel_tasks`/old-4 case still hardcodes the committed-layer command:

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

This ignores the layer of `schedule.parallel`. If the user's local layer contains `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (the intent explicitly supports setting these knobs in the git-ignored local layer, e.g. `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6`), then the local value overrides whatever the committed file says. Concretely:

1. Committed `.ddflow/config.toml` (written by an old `adopt`) has `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4` — the finding fires because the effective value is 4 and it is explicit.
2. `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (user opted into adaptive on this machine).
3. The note tells the user: "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`".
4. Running it writes `parallel = "fixed"` into the committed layer, which is overridden by the local `auto`, so the effective mode stays auto and the promised "keep exactly 4" is not achieved — the suggested command is a silent no-op.

The correct remedy (and the one the rest of the change establishes as the rule) is `_set_cmd(cfg, "schedule.parallel", "fixed")`, yielding `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` in this scenario. chunk_findings.detail:
The old call site was:

```python
_range_problems(repo, text, local) - _range_problems(repo, text_before, local)
```

where each `_range_problems` wrapped its `_effective` call in `except Exception: return set()`. The new code computes `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` **outside** any `try`, and catches only `(ValueError, OSError)` around the `before` evaluation. Both the pre-edit and post-edit evaluations have therefore lost the blanket `except Exception`.

Concrete failure: a project whose on-disk config makes `_effective` raise something outside `(ValueError, OSError)` — e.g. the project's `ConfigError` raised for an invalid `[schedule]` value such as `parallel = "bogus"` (the caller catches `ConfigError` separately from `(TOMLDecodeError, ValueError)`, so it is not necessarily a `ValueError`). A user then runs the *repair* edit, `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel auto`, which makes the after-text pass `Config.check`, so execution reaches `_new_range_problems`. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` succeeds, but the guarded call `_range_problems(repo, before, local)` raises `ConfigError`, which is not in `(ValueError, OSError)`, so it escapes and `ddflow config` aborts with a traceback instead of writing the repair. The docstring explicitly promises the opposite ("When the config before the edit cannot be judged, nothing can be attributed to the edit and nothing is refused"), and the old `except Exception` did allow exactly this repair. The same regression applies to the unguarded `found` line: any pre-edit failure mode of `_effective` that the old code swallowed for the after-text now propagates.

(Not reported: the flowparams fixed-mode mapping and the `min<=start<=max` handling, which look correct given the stated validation, and the README/doc-string requirements, which cannot be judged from this diff.)

The new `_doc()` entry documents the default for `schedule.parallel` as `"fixed"`:

```python
"schedule.parallel": (
    "fixed",

The entry should read `"auto"`, or the actual default and the test expectation must be changed to `fixed`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_range_problems` swallows every `Exception` with `return set()`, and its stated justification ("a text that does not load is Config.check's to report") is false at both call sites: the function is only invoked *after* `tomllib.loads` + `Config.check` have already succeeded. So any exception that escapes here is either a real bug or an unexpectedly unloadable *merged* config, not a load error, and it is silently converted into "this text has no range problems". Because callers then do `after - before`, the empty set is asymmetric and produces two concrete wrong outcomes:

1. If the "before" side raises while the "after" side succeeds, `after - set()` is the *entire* problem set of the effective config, so every pre-existing inconsistency is reclassified as "new" and an unrelated edit is refused — the exact opposite of the documented "a project whose range was already inconsistent can still make an unrelated edit, or the repair". E.g. a project whose committed/effective range is already inconsistent plus a local layer that currently fails to load: running `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` computes `before = set()` (the broken local text makes `_effective` raise), `after = <the pre-existing problems>` and returns `KeyRefused`, so the user cannot even repair the file.

2. If the "after" side raises while "before" succeeds, `new_range = set() - before` is empty and a genuinely newly inconsistent edit (e.g. `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 999`, giving `start > max` in the merged config) is accepted, writing a config that later commands must reject — i.e. the range guard is silently disabled exactly when it is supposed to fire.

`parallel_range_problems` and `_effective` are the only things reachable here; a bug or a cross-layer failure in either should surface, not be reported as "no problems". chunk_findings.detail: The new doctor advisories decide whether a cap is "explicit" with `_explicit`, which is true for *any* non-default source layer (`cfg.sources.get(key, "default") != "default"`), including the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer. But the remedy command they emit is layer-blind: it always writes the committed layer. Concretely, take a 4-core machine whose machine sizing was put in the local layer as instructed (`ddflow config --local --set worktree.max_parallel 4`). `_explicit` returns true and the value equals `OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT`, so the finding fires and prints "`ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` follows the schedule limit instead". Running exactly that command writes `.ddflow/config.toml` to 0, but the local layer wins for sizing, so `cfg.worktree.max_parallel` stays 4: the auto cap is unchanged and the doctor keeps firing forever with a command that cannot silence it. The remedy needs to target the layer the value actually lives in (e.g. `ddflow config --local --set worktree.max_parallel 0` when the source is the local layer). chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. Concrete scenario: editing the committed layer with `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` while the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer is unreadable (`chmod 000`) or malformed; the edited text passes `Config.check`, then `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` merges the broken local layer and raises `OSError`/`ValueError`, which now propagates out of `_new_range_problems` uncaught instead of being swallowed. Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new test asserts that `_new_range_problems(repo, "", "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
", True) == set()`, i.e. that the range guard reports *no* problem for a start value of 10 while the sibling layer is a syntactically broken TOML file. But the ceiling that makes 10 invalid is the shipped default `schedule.max_parallel_max = 8`, which does not live in the unreadable layer at all — it is knowable independently of it. The pre-existing test in the same file (`assert _new_range_problems(repo, "", after, False)` with `after = "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
"`) already shows that this exact value/`before=""` combination is supposed to be flagged as out of range. So the new test enshrines a behavior where a single TOML syntax error anywhere in the committed layer silently disables the ceiling check for a different key: `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 10` (or `--set schedule.max_parallel_max 3` etc.) is accepted instead of being reported, contradicting the stated requirement that out-of-range schedule knobs produce a config error (exit 3) naming the key. The correct defensive behavior is to swallow the parse failure only as far as avoiding a crash and to keep validating against the package-default floor/ceiling (and to let the normal config-load path surface the broken layer as exit 3); returning `set()` unconditionally on sibling read failure drops the range invariant entirely.

chunk_findings.detail: Every entry in this `(value, why)` doc table pairs a knob with its shipped default and a sentence describing what that default does: `schedule.cycle_policy` → `("error", …)`, `schedule.unknown_dep_policy` → `("block", …)`, `schedule.empty_phase` → `("problem", …)`, `dedupe.on_match` → `("ask", …)`, `enforce.commit_without_lease` → `("block", …)` — in each case the first element is exactly the default the package ships. The new `_doc()` entry documents the default for `schedule.parallel` as `"fixed"`:

"schedule.parallel": (
    "fixed",

So on a config with no `schedule.parallel` key, the effective behavior is `auto` (adaptive), yet `ddflow config --explain` (and any consumer that reads the first element as the documented default) reports `fixed`. chunk_findings.detail:
`_range_problems` swallows every `Exception` with `return set()`, and its stated justification ("a text that does not load is Config.check's to report") is false at both call sites: the function is only invoked *after* `tomllib.loads` + `Config.check` have already succeeded. So any exception that escapes here is either a real bug or an unexpectedly unloadable *merged* config, not a load error, and it is silently converted into "this text has no range problems". Because callers then do `after - before`, the empty set is asymmetric and produces two concrete wrong outcomes:

1. If the "before" side raises while the "after" side succeeds, `after - set()` is the *entire* problem set of the effective config, so every pre-existing inconsistency is reclassified as "new" and an unrelated edit is refused — the exact opposite of the documented "a project whose range was already inconsistent can still make an unrelated edit, or the repair". E.g. a project whose committed/effective range is already inconsistent plus a local layer that currently fails to load: running `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` computes `before = set()` (the broken local text makes `_effective` raise), `after = <the pre-existing problems>` and returns `KeyRefused`, so the user cannot even repair the file.

2. If the "after" side raises while "before" succeeds, `new_range = set() - before` is empty and a genuinely newly inconsistent edit (e.g. `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 999`, giving `start > max` in the merged config) is accepted, writing a config that later commands must reject — i.e. the range guard is silently disabled exactly when it is supposed to fire.

`parallel_range_problems` and `_effective` are the only things reachable here; a bug or a cross-layer failure in either should surface, not be reported as "no problems". chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. Concrete scenario: editing the committed layer with `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` while the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer is unreadable (`chmod 000`) or malformed; the edited text passes `Config.check`, then `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` merges the broken local layer and raises `OSError`/`ValueError`, which now propagates out of `_new_range_problems` uncaught instead of being swallowed. Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

This ignores the layer of `schedule.parallel`. If the user's local layer contains `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (the intent explicitly supports setting these knobs in the git-ignored local layer, e.g. `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6`), then the local value overrides whatever the committed file says. Concretely:

1. Committed `.ddflow/config.toml` (written by an old `adopt`) has `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4` — the finding fires because the effective value is 4 and it is explicit.
2. `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (user opted into adaptive on this machine).
3. The note tells the user: "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`".
4. Running it writes `parallel = "fixed"` into the committed layer, which is overridden by the local `auto`, so the effective mode stays auto and the promised "keep exactly 4" is not achieved — the suggested command is a silent no-op.

The correct remedy (and the one the rest of the change establishes as the rule) is `_set_cmd(cfg, "schedule.parallel", "fixed")`, yielding `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` in this scenario. The changed tests only cover the layer-aware path for `worktree.max_parallel` (`test_a_local_cap_is_given_a_local_remedy`); no test exercises a local `schedule.parallel`, so this gap passes CI.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new test asserts that `_new_range_problems(repo, "", "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
", True) == set()`, i.e. that the range guard reports *no* problem for a start value of 10 while the sibling layer is a syntactically broken TOML file. But the ceiling that makes 10 invalid is the shipped default `schedule.max_parallel_max = 8`, which does not live in the unreadable layer at all — it is knowable independently of it. The pre-existing test in the same file (`assert _new_range_problems(repo, "", after, False)` with `after = "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
"`) already shows that this exact value/`before=""` combination is supposed to be flagged as out of range. So the new test enshrines a behavior where a single TOML syntax error anywhere in the committed layer silently disables the ceiling check for a different key: `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 10` (or `--set schedule.max_parallel_max 3` etc.) is accepted instead of being reported, contradicting the stated requirement that out-of-range schedule knobs produce a config error (exit 3) naming the key. The correct defensive behavior is to swallow the parse failure only as far as avoiding a crash and to keep validating against the package-default floor/ceiling (and to let the normal config-load path surface the broken layer as exit 3); returning `set()` unconditionally on sibling read failure drops the range invariant entirely.

chunk_findings.detail:
The remedy command's layer is now chosen from the layer of `schedule.max_parallel_tasks`, but the command *sets* `schedule.parallel`, whose effective layer is decided by `schedule.parallel` itself. When the two keys live in different layers, the printed command no longer does what the message promises.

Concrete failure: committed `.ddflow/config.toml` contains the old adopted default `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4`, and `.ddflow/local/config.toml` contains `[schedule] parallel = "auto"` (a per-machine override, exactly the case the feature advertises: "a local-layer value overrides the committed one"). The finding fires (effective `parallel` is auto and `max_parallel_tasks` is the old default), and the tail of the message offers "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`" — because `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.max_parallel_tasks')` is false, no `--local` is emitted. Running that command writes `parallel = fixed` into the committed layer, which the pre-existing local `parallel = "auto"` still overrides, so the effective value stays `auto` and the limit can still rise above 4. The user cannot reach the state the message describes.

This is a regression from the pre-change behavior: `_set_cmd(cfg, 'schedule.parallel', 'fixed')` checked `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.parallel')`, which is true here, so it emitted `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` and actually took effect. The new `layer_of` argument also contradicts its own docstring ("a machine's own override must not be answered in the shared file") in this case: the machine's override is on `schedule.parallel`, and the answer is placed in the shared file anyway. The fix should key the layer off the key being set, or off whichever of the two keys is more specific (local wins), rather than unconditionally off `layer_of`.

chunk_findings.detail: Every entry in this `(value, why)` doc table pairs a knob with its shipped default and a sentence describing what that default does: `schedule.cycle_policy` → `("error", …)`, `schedule.unknown_dep_policy` → `("block", …)`, `schedule.empty_phase` → `("problem", …)`, `dedupe.on_match` → `("ask", …)`, `enforce.commit_without_lease` → `("block", …)` — in each case the first element is exactly the default the package ships. The change under review, however, registers `"schedule.parallel": ("fixed", "no safety dimension; changes least -- max_parallel_tasks is the number, nothing adapts")`, while the intent and the choice tuple added two lines earlier (`("auto", "fixed")`) define the default as `auto`. So `ddflow config --explain` will report `schedule.parallel`'s default as `fixed`, i.e. it will tell users that adaptation is off by default when the shipped default is `auto`; and any doc-coverage check that cross-validates the documented value against the `ScheduleConfig` default (or against the first member of the choices tuple) is comparing `fixed` to `auto` and cannot pass. The fix is to make the pair `("auto", …)` with a sentence describing the auto default.

chunk_findings.detail: `params()` never reads `cfg.schedule.parallel`, so it cannot encode the required "fixed" semantics (intent: `parallel` is `auto|fixed`; `max_parallel_tasks` is "the start value in auto, **the number in fixed**", and "fixed + 4 reproduces the old behaviour"). Given a config with `parallel = "fixed"`, `max_parallel_tasks = 4`, `max_parallel_min = 2`, `max_parallel_max = 8`, the call returns `FC.Params(start=4, floor=2, ceiling=8, ...)`, i.e. a controller that is free to move the limit anywhere in `[2, 8]`. The operator asked for exactly 4, so the run does not reproduce the old fixed-4 behaviour and can exceed or fall below it. The module's own docstring says this is "the one place that turns the operator's knobs into its `Params`, so every caller (the sampler, `plan`, the operator surface) folds with the same numbers" — meaning fixed mode must be neutralised here (e.g. `floor=ceiling=start` when `s.parallel == "fixed"`); nothing else in this change does it, and the corresponding `fixed + 4` acceptance test cannot pass through this path.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_explicit()` returns True for a key whose source is anything other than `"default"`, including a value that lives in the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer. The advisory's remedy, however, is always the non-`--local` command:

```
"... clean it ... `ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` follows the schedule limit instead ..."
```

Since the change itself establishes that "a local-layer value overrides the committed one" and that `--local` is what selects the local layer, running `ddflow config --set worktree.max_parallel 0` writes the committed layer while the local `worktree.max_parallel = 4` still wins. Concrete scenario: a machine has `[worktree] max_parallel = 4` only in `.ddflow/local` (exactly the "machine-specific value goes to the local layer" case the intent prescribes). On that host the effective `cfg.worktree.max_parallel` is 4 and its source is `local`, so this finding fires and prints the remedy. The operator runs it, no error is reported, and the cap silently stays at 4 — the doctor claims to have given "the exact remedy command" but the command is a no-op for this input. The same defect applies to the `max_parallel_tasks` advisory ("to accept auto, remove the line"): when the old explicit 4 lives in the local layer, removing the committed line does nothing. The code has the source string available (it was just used by `_explicit`) but never uses it to pick `--local` in the message.

chunk_findings.detail: The edited tests inject `max_parallel_tasks = 1` into `[schedule]` while leaving the shipped default `max_parallel_min = 2` in place. The change's own stated validation is "min<=start<=max, min>=1; invalid -> config error exit 3 naming the key", and `max_parallel_tasks` is the start value in `parallel='auto'` (which is exactly what these tests rely on, since they only add the one key). With start=1 and min=2 the config is invalid, so `run_cli(...)` will exit 3 at config load and none of the assertions that follow (claim U1 succeeds, U2/U3 are refused, "any release frees a slot", word-for-word cap wording, etc.) can run; the tests `"N more are ready" read as a contradiction` and the `_blocking_leases` wording test cannot exercise the cap-1 case at all. If instead the implementation silently clamps the start up into `[min,max]`, the effective cap becomes 2, which is equally wrong for these tests' expectation of a single startable item. Either way these hunks are only correct if `max_parallel_min` is also lowered to 1 (e.g. add `max_parallel_min = 1` alongside `max_parallel_tasks = 1`), which the diff does not do.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call site was:

```python
_range_problems(repo, text, local) - _range_problems(repo, text_before, local)
```

where each `_range_problems` wrapped its `_effective` call in `except Exception: return set()`. The new code computes `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` **outside** any `try`, and catches only `(ValueError, OSError)` around the `before` evaluation. Both the pre-edit and post-edit evaluations have therefore lost the blanket `except Exception`.

Concrete failure: a project whose on-disk config makes `_effective` raise something outside `(ValueError, OSError)` — e.g. the project's `ConfigError` raised for an invalid `[schedule]` value such as `parallel = "bogus"` (the caller catches `ConfigError` separately from `(TOMLDecodeError, ValueError)`, so it is not necessarily a `ValueError`). A user then runs the *repair* edit, `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel auto`, which makes the after-text pass `Config.check`, so execution reaches `_new_range_problems`. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` succeeds, but the guarded call `_range_problems(repo, before, local)` raises `ConfigError`, which is not in `(ValueError, OSError)`, so it escapes and `ddflow config` aborts with a traceback instead of writing the repair. The docstring explicitly promises the opposite ("When the config before the edit cannot be judged, nothing can be attributed to the edit and nothing is refused"), and the old `except Exception` did allow exactly this repair. The same regression applies to the unguarded `found` line: any pre-edit failure mode of `_effective` that the old code swallowed for the after-text now propagates.

(Not reported: the flowparams fixed-mode mapping and the `min<=start<=max` handling, which look correct given the stated validation, and the README/doc-string requirements, which cannot be judged from this diff.)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_set_cmd` helper is applied to the `worktree.max_parallel` remedy and the file-name half of the `schedule.max_parallel_tasks` message, but the sibling remedy in the same sentence is still hardcoded to the committed layer:

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

Because the change explicitly makes every schedule knob settable in the git-ignored local layer and states "a local-layer value overrides the committed one", `schedule.parallel` can legitimately live in that layer, and the hardcoded `--set` then targets the wrong layer. Concrete input: `.ddflow/local/config.toml` contains

    [schedule]
    parallel = "auto"

and `.ddflow/config.toml` contains

    [schedule]
    max_parallel_tasks = 4

The finding fires (`max_parallel_tasks` is explicit and equals the old default, effective mode is `auto`), and its detail tells the operator to run `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`. That writes `parallel = "fixed"` into the committed file, but the local `parallel = "auto"` still wins, so the effective mode stays `auto` and the limit can still rise to `schedule.max_parallel_max` — exactly what the message claims to prevent. The remedy should be produced by `_set_cmd(cfg, "schedule.parallel", "fixed")`, which would emit `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` in this case, consistent with the layer-aware logic introduced for the other two remedies.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new test enshrines a validation bypass rather than merely "not crashing". It writes an unparsable committed layer (`"[schedule
"`) and then asserts that `_new_range_problems(repo, "", "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
", True) == set()`. The pre-existing test immediately above it shows that the *same* `before=""` / `after="[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
"` input is a range problem when the sibling layer is healthy (the earlier assertion `_new_range_problems(repo, "", after, False)` is truthy). So with a healthy committed layer, `max_parallel_tasks = 10` exceeds the default ceiling (`max_parallel_max = 8`) and is refused; with a committed layer that merely contains a TOML syntax error, the identical out-of-range write to the local layer is accepted with no problems at all. That contradicts the stated requirement that out-of-range values are invalid and must fail with a config error (exit 3): a user (or a scripted `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 10`) can neutralize the range guard entirely by first corrupting the sibling layer, and the invalid value is written instead of rejected. The safe behaviour when the sibling cannot be read is to fall back to the built-in defaults and still flag `10 > 8`; catching the parse error and returning an empty problem set silently disables the check exactly in the case where the guard is most needed.

chunk_findings.detail: When `local` is False (a committed-layer write) the handler is a no-op retry: the first call `_range_problems(repo, after, local)` fails, and the fallback then calls `_range_problems(repo, after, False)` with exactly the same arguments. The same deterministic failure repeats, and this second call is not inside a `try`, so it propagates. Concrete input: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed` with a valid committed `.ddflow/config.toml` but a malformed `.ddflow/local/config.toml`; the first call raises `TOMLDecodeError`, the fallback raises the identical `TOMLDecodeError` again, and the writer crashes with a traceback instead of refusing nothing. The old `except Exception: return set()` deliberately avoided this; the new fallback only rescues the `local=True` orientation, not the `local=False` one.

The layer must follow the key being set (`schedule.parallel`), or at minimum the union of both layers, rather than only `max_parallel_tasks`.

chunk_findings.detail: `params()` never reads `cfg.schedule.parallel`, so a `fixed` schedule is translated into the same adaptive parameter set as `auto`. chunk_findings.detail:
`_range_problems` swallows every `Exception` with `return set()`, and its stated justification ("a text that does not load is Config.check's to report") is false at both call sites: the function is only invoked *after* `tomllib.loads` + `Config.check` have already succeeded. So any exception that escapes here is either a real bug or an unexpectedly unloadable *merged* config, not a load error, and it is silently converted into "this text has no range problems". Because callers then do `after - before`, the empty set is asymmetric and produces two concrete wrong outcomes:

1. If the "before" side raises while the "after" side succeeds, `after - set()` is the *entire* problem set of the effective config, so every pre-existing inconsistency is reclassified as "new" and an unrelated edit is refused — the exact opposite of the documented "a project whose range was already inconsistent can still make an unrelated edit, or the repair". E.g. a project whose committed/effective range is already inconsistent plus a local layer that currently fails to load: running `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` computes `before = set()` (the broken local text makes `_effective` raise), `after = <the pre-existing problems>` and returns `KeyRefused`, so the user cannot even repair the file.

2. If the "after" side raises while "before" succeeds, `new_range = set() - before` is empty and a genuinely newly inconsistent edit (e.g. `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 999`, giving `start > max` in the merged config) is accepted, writing a config that later commands must reject — i.e. the range guard is silently disabled exactly when it is supposed to fire.

`parallel_range_problems` and `_effective` are the only things reachable here; a bug or a cross-layer failure in either should surface, not be reported as "no problems". chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. Concrete scenario: editing the committed layer with `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` while the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer is unreadable (`chmod 000`) or malformed; the edited text passes `Config.check`, then `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` merges the broken local layer and raises `OSError`/`ValueError`, which now propagates out of `_new_range_problems` uncaught instead of being swallowed. Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The detail string for the explicit-`max_parallel_tasks`/old-4 case still hardcodes the committed-layer command:

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

This ignores the layer of `schedule.parallel`. If the user's local layer contains `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (the intent explicitly supports setting these knobs in the git-ignored local layer, e.g. `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6`), then the local value overrides whatever the committed file says. Concretely:

1. Committed `.ddflow/config.toml` (written by an old `adopt`) has `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4` — the finding fires because the effective value is 4 and it is explicit.
2. `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (user opted into adaptive on this machine).
3. The note tells the user: "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`".
4. Running it writes `parallel = "fixed"` into the committed layer, which is overridden by the local `auto`, so the effective mode stays auto and the promised "keep exactly 4" is not achieved — the suggested command is a silent no-op.

The correct remedy (and the one the rest of the change establishes as the rule) is `_set_cmd(cfg, "schedule.parallel", "fixed")`, yielding `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` in this scenario. The changed tests only cover the layer-aware path for `worktree.max_parallel` (`test_a_local_cap_is_given_a_local_remedy`); no test exercises a local `schedule.parallel`, so this gap passes CI.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workflow.py:_parallel_findings (the `schedule.max_parallel_tasks` note)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new test asserts that `_new_range_problems(repo, "", "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
", True) == set()`, i.e. that the range guard reports *no* problem for a start value of 10 while the sibling layer is a syntactically broken TOML file. But the ceiling that makes 10 invalid is the shipped default `schedule.max_parallel_max = 8`, which does not live in the unreadable layer at all — it is knowable independently of it. The pre-existing test in the same file (`assert _new_range_problems(repo, "", after, False)` with `after = "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
"`) already shows that this exact value/`before=""` combination is supposed to be flagged as out of range. So the new test enshrines a behavior where a single TOML syntax error anywhere in the committed layer silently disables the ceiling check for a different key: `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 10` (or `--set schedule.max_parallel_max 3` etc.) is accepted instead of being reported, contradicting the stated requirement that out-of-range schedule knobs produce a config error (exit 3) naming the key. The correct defensive behavior is to swallow the parse failure only as far as avoiding a crash and to keep validating against the package-default floor/ceiling (and to let the normal config-load path surface the broken layer as exit 3); returning `set()` unconditionally on sibling read failure drops the range invariant entirely.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adaptive_config.py :: test_an_unreadable_sibling_layer_never_crashes_the_range_guard

chunk_findings.detail:
The remedy command's layer is now chosen from the layer of `schedule.max_parallel_tasks`, but the command *sets* `schedule.parallel`, whose effective layer is decided by `schedule.parallel` itself. When the two keys live in different layers, the printed command no longer does what the message promises.

Concrete failure: committed `.ddflow/config.toml` contains the old adopted default `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4`, and `.ddflow/local/config.toml` contains `[schedule] parallel = "auto"` (a per-machine override, exactly the case the feature advertises: "a local-layer value overrides the committed one"). The finding fires (effective `parallel` is auto and `max_parallel_tasks` is the old default), and the tail of the message offers "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`" — because `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.max_parallel_tasks')` is false, no `--local` is emitted. Running that command writes `parallel = fixed` into the committed layer, which the pre-existing local `parallel = "auto"` still overrides, so the effective value stays `auto` and the limit can still rise above 4. The user cannot reach the state the message describes.

This is a regression from the pre-change behavior: `_set_cmd(cfg, 'schedule.parallel', 'fixed')` checked `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.parallel')`, which is true here, so it emitted `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` and actually took effect. The new `layer_of` argument also contradicts its own docstring ("a machine's own override must not be answered in the shared file") in this case: the machine's override is on `schedule.parallel`, and the answer is placed in the shared file anyway. The fix should key the layer off the key being set, or off whichever of the two keys is more specific (local wins), rather than unconditionally off `layer_of`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workflow.py `_set_cmd` call inside `_parallel_findings` (`layer_of='schedule.max_parallel_tasks'`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new code conflates two different causes of `judged(after, local) is None`: the *sibling* (committed) layer being unreadable, and the *edit text* `after` itself being unreadable. In the old code the sibling-broken case was handled by `found = _range_problems(repo, after, False)` (which succeeds only because `after` was assumed to parse), and if `after` itself could not be loaded that second call raised `unreadable` out of `_new_range_problems`, so the caller saw the failure. In the new code the retry is wrapped as `judged(after, False) or set()`: for an edit text that does not load, `judged(after, False)` is again `None`, so `found` becomes `set()`, `had` is subtracted from it, and the function returns the empty set — i.e. "this edit introduces no new problems". Demonstration: with a valid committed layer and `before` valid, call `_new_range_problems(repo, before, '[schedule]\nmax_parallel_min = "x"\n', True)`. `judged(after, True)` raises (bad type raises `ValueError`, exactly as the new test relies on for `adapt_up_after_s = "x"`), `local` is flipped to `False`, and the retry over the defaults raises the same way, so the result is `set()`. `_range_refusal(set())` then yields no refusal and the caller is free to write a layer whose merged config cannot load; previously that failure propagated. The added test only exercises an unloadable *before*, so this path is untested, and the docstring's own principle ("a broken sibling never switches the guard off") is violated in the other direction: a broken edit text silently switches the range guard off.

chunk_findings.detail: The sampler is invoked as `FL.sample_if_due(ctx, SIG.HostSignals(repo))` — two arguments — while the API this change introduces (and that the failing-first tests exercise) is `sample_if_due(ctx, source, clock)`: an injected clock is an explicit parameter, which is exactly why the tests can drive it deterministically. Because the call omits the `clock` argument and the whole block is wrapped in `except Exception: return`, any `TypeError` raised by a signature where `clock` has no default is silently discarded. Concrete failure: run `ddflow brief` (or `next`/`claim`/`heartbeat`) on a fresh project in `auto` mode past `schedule.signal_interval_s`; `_load` reaches this line, `sample_if_due` is called with a missing positional argument, the exception is swallowed, and `.ddflow/local/flow/samples.jsonl` is never appended to — so the ring stays empty and `current_limit` never folds in any new sample, leaving the "adaptive" limit permanently at its start value. The unit tests do not catch this because they call `sample_if_due` directly with their injected clock rather than going through `_load`, so CI is green while production sampling is dead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/_base.py:_sample_flow

chunk_findings.detail: `read_ring` skips a truncated final line, but `sample_if_due` then appends the next sample to that same line instead of repairing it, and the ring can never recover. Concretely: if a write is cut short (process killed mid-flush, or the disk fills mid-append at lines 216-217) the file ends with a partial record and no trailing `\n`, e.g. `{"at": 1.0, "signals": {"gate`. On the next call `read_ring` line 83-87 fails `json.loads` on this line and returns `rows == []`, so `kept == rows == []` and the condition on line 215 (`len(kept) == len(rows) and path.exists()`) selects the plain-append branch; the new, well-formed record is written immediately after the partial one with no separator, producing a single line that `json.loads` also rejects. `read_ring` therefore keeps returning `[]`, the trim branch is never taken (it needs `len(kept) != len(rows)`), and every subsequent sample is silently swallowed while `sample_if_due` still returns `SampleResult(True)`. The adaptive limit is thus permanently pinned at its start value (and `doctor_notes` reports nothing, since the file is readable and the directory is writable) until someone deletes the ring by hand. The intended "tolerates a corrupt or truncated line (skips it)" behaviour is not achieved: a corrupt line is only skipped on read, not excluded from the file, so a *truncated* line poisons the ring for good.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/flowstate.py:215 (append branch, with read_ring at :83)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `".ddflow/local" not in status` cannot detect the failure it is written to catch. `repo` is a freshly-initialised git repo with no tracked files under `.ddflow/`, so if `sample_if_due` fails to create `.ddflow/local/.gitignore` and the ring is left unignored, `git status --porcelain` (default `status.showUntrackedFiles=normal`) collapses the whole untracked tree to a single entry `?? .ddflow/`. The substring `.ddflow/local` is not present in `?? .ddflow/`, so the test passes even though the ring is committable — exactly the "nothing under `.ddflow/local/` is ever staged" property it claims to guard. It only accidentally fails on machines/CI where `status.showUntrackedFiles=all` (or `-uall`) is configured, in which case the output becomes `?? .ddflow/local/flow/samples.jsonl` and the assertion trips for environmental reasons, not for the intended reason. Either way the check is not testing the lazy self-ignore behaviour.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_flowstate.py::test_without_init_the_local_dir_ignores_itself

chunk_findings.detail: `_sample_flow` is invoked from the shared `_load` path, and it evaluates `log.read_all()` and constructs `SIG.HostSignals(repo)` before handing anything to `FL.sample_if_due`. The interval throttle lives inside `sample_if_due`, so it only suppresses the *append*: the expensive prerequisites run on every single `_load`, i.e. on every `next`, `brief`, `claim` and `heartbeat`. Given a project whose `.ddflow` event log has grown large, an invocation that is well inside `schedule.signal_interval_s` (so no sample is due) still reads the entire event log — exactly the work the "throttled opportunistic sampling" design says should be skipped. A user running `ddflow next` in a loop would pay a full log read per call even though `samples.jsonl` is written at most once per interval. The throttle check needs to happen (or at least the `events`/`HostSignals` construction needs to be deferred) before the log is read and host signals are probed, so that a not-due invocation does no more than a cheap stat/read of the ring.

chunk_findings.detail:
`read_ring` deliberately skips a corrupt/truncated final line, but the normal write path never repairs the file: it appends to it. If `samples.jsonl`'s last physical line has no trailing newline — exactly what a crash-mid-write produces, and also what you get if the file was last touched by the trim path being interrupted or by any external editor — the code still takes the append branch, because `kept`/`rows` are derived only from the well-formed lines and `path.exists()` is true. So `{"at":100,..."signals":{}}` (no `
`) plus a new sample becomes `{"at":100,...}{"at":200,...}
`. On the next `read_ring`, both objects are on one line, `json.loads` fails, and *both* the just-written sample and the previously valid sample are silently dropped — while `sample_if_due` returns `SampleResult(True)`. This breaks the stated "tolerates a corrupt or truncated line" guarantee and loses a good sample. A concrete repro: write a ring whose only content is `{"at": 1, "signals": {}}` with no newline, call `sample_if_due` twice with an advancing clock, and `read_ring` returns an empty list; the second call also returns `written=True` even though nothing parseable was added. The fix is to ensure the file ends in `
` (or to route through the rewrite branch whenever the on-disk text does not end with a newline).

chunk_findings.detail: The stale-lock takeover unlinks a lock it did not create, and the `finally` unconditionally unlinks `lock` regardless of who currently owns that path. Under a wall-clock jump forward — NTP correction, or suspend/resume, which `time.time()`-based staleness cannot distinguish from a crashed sampler — a second sampler B can declare A's live lock stale (age > `STALE_LOCK_S`), unlink it, create its own lock and enter the critical section, while A is still inside it. When A finishes, A's `finally` calls `lock.unlink()` and deletes *B's* lock file, so a third sampler C can immediately acquire a fresh lock and run concurrently with B. Both then append to / `os.replace` the ring without mutual exclusion, which is precisely the "two agents sampling concurrently never corrupt it" property the change is supposed to guarantee. The trigger is a sample that holds the lock longer than 10 s (large event log in `_log_signals`/`source.sample()`, or a suspended process), which is why the hold time (`LOCK_WAIT_S`=2 s) and the staleness threshold (`STALE_LOCK_S`=10 s) do not protect it. Ownership should be checked before unlinking (e.g., compare the lock's inode/token) rather than unlinking the path unconditionally.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new stale-lock takeover is a TOCTOU race that can delete a *fresh* lock, contradicting its own docstring ("only one taker's rename can succeed, so a fresh lock is never removed by mistake"). The `stale` decision is made from an earlier `lock.stat()`, but the `os.rename(lock, aside)` is performed later and is not conditional on the source still being the same inode. Concrete interleaving with a crashed owner C leaving a stale lock L:

1. Process A: `stat(L)` is stale → proceeds to rename.
2. Process B: `stat(L)` is stale (also read before A renames) → proceeds to rename.
3. A: `os.rename(L, aside-A)` succeeds; `aside-A.unlink()`; `continue`; A's `os.open(L, O_EXCL|O_CREAT)` succeeds and A now holds the lock.
4. B: `os.rename(L, aside-B)` now renames **A's fresh lock** (the path was recreated), then `aside-B.unlink()` — A's lock silently disappears while A still believes it holds it.

Now a third sampler E can acquire `L` and run concurrently with A, so two writers can append to `samples.jsonl` in the critical section the lock was supposed to guard. The rename must be made conditional on the file still being the stale one (e.g. rename to a unique name and re-verify the inode/mtime before unlinking, or use an atomic compare-and-swap), otherwise the stated "two agents sampling concurrently never corrupt it" guarantee does not hold.

chunk_findings.detail:
`read_ring` deliberately skips a corrupt/truncated final line, but the normal write path never repairs the file: it appends to it. So `{"at":100,..."signals":{}}` (no `
`) plus a new sample becomes `{"at":100,...}{"at":200,...}
`. On the next `read_ring`, both objects are on one line, `json.loads` fails, and *both* the just-written sample and the previously valid sample are silently dropped — while `sample_if_due` returns `SampleResult(True)`. This breaks the stated "tolerates a corrupt or truncated line" guarantee and loses a good sample. The fix is to ensure the file ends in `
` (or to route through the rewrite branch whenever the on-disk text does not end with a newline).

chunk_findings.detail: The stale-lock takeover unlinks a lock it did not create, and the `finally` unconditionally unlinks `lock` regardless of who currently owns that path. Under a wall-clock jump forward — NTP correction, or suspend/resume, which `time.time()`-based staleness cannot distinguish from a crashed sampler — a second sampler B can declare A's live lock stale (age > `STALE_LOCK_S`), unlink it, create its own lock and enter the critical section, while A is still inside it. When A finishes, A's `finally` calls `lock.unlink()` and deletes *B's* lock file, so a third sampler C can immediately acquire a fresh lock and run concurrently with B. Both then append to / `os.replace` the ring without mutual exclusion, which is precisely the "two agents sampling concurrently never corrupt it" property the change is supposed to guarantee. The trigger is a sample that holds the lock longer than 10 s (large event log in `_log_signals`/`source.sample()`, or a suspended process), which is why the hold time (`LOCK_WAIT_S`=2 s) and the staleness threshold (`STALE_LOCK_S`=10 s) do not protect it. Ownership should be checked before unlinking (e.g., compare the lock's inode/token) rather than unlinking the path unconditionally.

chunk_findings.detail: `_append_line` claims to perform "one `O_APPEND` write of one whole line", but it calls `os.write(fd, line.encode("utf-8"))` and discards the return value. `os.write` is documented to return the number of bytes actually written, which may be *less* than the buffer length (interrupted by a signal after a partial transfer, `ENOSPC`/`EDQUOT` on a full or quota-limited filesystem, or certain network filesystems). When that happens, only a prefix of the line reaches the file and the remainder is never written: the ring gains a truncated JSON line. This is exactly the failure the change's docstring says it prevents ("no interleaving tears a line") and that the new test asserts never occurs (`json.loads(line)` over every line). The previous implementation used a text-mode file object, whose buffering re-issues the write until the whole line is out, so this is a regression introduced by the change. Demonstration: run the sampler on a filesystem where `os.write` returns a short count (e.g. near-`ENOSPC`, or a source that race-injects `os.write` returning `len(data)//2`); the resulting `samples.jsonl` contains a line that fails `json.loads`, which `read_ring` will then silently skip — losing the sample and contradicting the "torn line" guarantee. Writing the line via a loop until all bytes are consumed (or `os.fdopen(fd, "a", encoding="utf-8").write(...)`) restores the guarantee.

chunk_findings.detail: The sampler is invoked as `FL.sample_if_due(ctx, SIG.HostSignals(repo))` — two arguments — while the API this change introduces (and that the failing-first tests exercise) is `sample_if_due(ctx, source, clock)`: an injected clock is an explicit parameter, which is exactly why the tests can drive it deterministically. Because the call omits the `clock` argument and the whole block is wrapped in `except Exception: return`, any `TypeError` raised by a signature where `clock` has no default is silently discarded. Concrete failure: run `ddflow brief` (or `next`/`claim`/`heartbeat`) on a fresh project in `auto` mode past `schedule.signal_interval_s`; `_load` reaches this line, `sample_if_due` is called with a missing positional argument, the exception is swallowed, and `.ddflow/local/flow/samples.jsonl` is never appended to — so the ring stays empty and `current_limit` never folds in any new sample, leaving the "adaptive" limit permanently at its start value. The unit tests do not catch this because they call `sample_if_due` directly with their injected clock rather than going through `_load`, so CI is green while production sampling is dead.

chunk_findings.detail: `read_ring` skips a truncated final line, but `sample_if_due` then appends the next sample to that same line instead of repairing it, and the ring can never recover. Concretely: if a write is cut short (process killed mid-flush, or the disk fills mid-append at lines 216-217) the file ends with a partial record and no trailing `\n`, e.g. `{"at": 1.0, "signals": {"gate`. On the next call `read_ring` line 83-87 fails `json.loads` on this line and returns `rows == []`, so `kept == rows == []` and the condition on line 215 (`len(kept) == len(rows) and path.exists()`) selects the plain-append branch; the new, well-formed record is written immediately after the partial one with no separator, producing a single line that `json.loads` also rejects. `read_ring` therefore keeps returning `[]`, the trim branch is never taken (it needs `len(kept) != len(rows)`), and every subsequent sample is silently swallowed while `sample_if_due` still returns `SampleResult(True)`. The adaptive limit is thus permanently pinned at its start value (and `doctor_notes` reports nothing, since the file is readable and the directory is writable) until someone deletes the ring by hand. The intended "tolerates a corrupt or truncated line (skips it)" behaviour is not achieved: a corrupt line is only skipped on read, not excluded from the file, so a *truncated* line poisons the ring for good.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `".ddflow/local" not in status` cannot detect the failure it is written to catch. `repo` is a freshly-initialised git repo with no tracked files under `.ddflow/`, so if `sample_if_due` fails to create `.ddflow/local/.gitignore` and the ring is left unignored, `git status --porcelain` (default `status.showUntrackedFiles=normal`) collapses the whole untracked tree to a single entry `?? .ddflow/`. The substring `.ddflow/local` is not present in `?? .ddflow/`, so the test passes even though the ring is committable — exactly the "nothing under `.ddflow/local/` is ever staged" property it claims to guard. It only accidentally fails on machines/CI where `status.showUntrackedFiles=all` (or `-uall`) is configured, in which case the output becomes `?? .ddflow/local/flow/samples.jsonl` and the assertion trips for environmental reasons, not for the intended reason. Either way the check is not testing the lazy self-ignore behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new stale-lock takeover is a TOCTOU race that can delete a *fresh* lock, contradicting its own docstring ("only one taker's rename can succeed, so a fresh lock is never removed by mistake"). The `stale` decision is made from an earlier `lock.stat()`, but the `os.rename(lock, aside)` is performed later and is not conditional on the source still being the same inode. Concrete interleaving with a crashed owner C leaving a stale lock L:

1. Process A: `stat(L)` is stale → proceeds to rename.
2. Process B: `stat(L)` is stale (also read before A renames) → proceeds to rename.
3. A: `os.rename(L, aside-A)` succeeds; `aside-A.unlink()`; `continue`; A's `os.open(L, O_EXCL|O_CREAT)` succeeds and A now holds the lock.
4. B: `os.rename(L, aside-B)` now renames **A's fresh lock** (the path was recreated), then `aside-B.unlink()` — A's lock silently disappears while A still believes it holds it.

Now a third sampler E can acquire `L` and run concurrently with A, so two writers can append to `samples.jsonl` in the critical section the lock was supposed to guard. The rename must be made conditional on the file still being the stale one (e.g. rename to a unique name and re-verify the inode/mtime before unlinking, or use an atomic compare-and-swap), otherwise the stated "two agents sampling concurrently never corrupt it" guarantee does not hold.

chunk_findings.detail: The temp path is made unique only by `os.getpid()` + `time.time_ns()`: `tmp = path.with_name(f"{path.name}.{os.getpid()}-{time.time_ns()}.tmp")`. Two writers in the *same process* (threads) share the pid and can read the same `time.time_ns()` value, so they select the same temp file — which breaks the very invariant the new docstring claims ("a temporary file of the writer's own", "no interleaving tears a line"). The change's own test drives exactly this case: it monkeypatches `_lock` to a no-op and runs six `threading.Thread`s, all of which hit the replace branch on their first iteration (the file was just corrupted with `torn`), i.e. the same-pid collision window is deliberately opened by the new test. When two same-pid writers collide, both `os.open('w')` truncate to offset 0 and then both write their whole `body` from offset 0 without any mutual exclusion; because `write` does not truncate the file, if the writer that writes last has a shorter `body` than the one that wrote first, the ring file keeps the first writer's tail bytes past the second body's end — a mixed/torn line — and that mixed file is then installed with `os.replace(tmp, path)`. The other ordering (A replaces, then B's `os.replace` on the now-missing temp) raises `FileNotFoundError` out of `_replace` into `sample_if_due`, silently dropping that sample (and, in the test, the exception just dies in the worker thread because thread exceptions don't fail `join()`). A robust token must be unique per *writer*, not per process (e.g. `tempfile.mkstemp`/`uuid`/`threading.get_ident()`), otherwise the "lock only throttles; the file is safe without it" guarantee does not hold for the concurrent-sampling scenario this change is built around.

Given a project whose `.ddflow` event log has grown large, an invocation that is well inside `schedule.signal_interval_s` (so no sample is due) still reads the entire event log — exactly the work the "throttled opportunistic sampling" design says should be skipped. A user running `ddflow next` in a loop would pay a full log read per call even though `samples.jsonl` is written at most once per interval. The throttle check needs to happen (or at least the `events`/`HostSignals` construction needs to be deferred) before the log is read and host signals are probed, so that a not-due invocation does no more than a cheap stat/read of the ring.
